title: Where is it, which way
goal: Ask for directions and understand the answer — plus the Egyptian imperative, which is actually shorter than the ordinary verb form.
bekal: ask where places are and understand the directions you're given
tell and invite people to do things with the imperative

dialogs.title: حوار — تايه في وسط البلد
dialogs.intro: Budi is looking for a post office in Downtown Cairo. The map on his phone has lost signal, so he asks a newspaper seller on the street corner.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Excuse me, where's the post office?

lines.speaker: الراجل:
lines.text: البوسطة؟ قريبة. امشي على طول لحد الميدان.
lines.id: The post office? It's close. Walk straight on to the square.
lines.literal: the-post? close. walk on length until the-square.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Second street on the left. Okay.

lines.speaker: الراجل:
lines.text: حتلاقيها على إيدك اليمين، جنب الصيدلية.
lines.id: You'll find it on your right, next to the pharmacy.
lines.literal: you-will-find-it on your-hand the-right, beside the-pharmacy.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: And what time does it close?

lines.speaker: الراجل:
lines.id: Three in the afternoon. Better hurry!

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: It's a quarter to three now!

lines.speaker: الراجل:
lines.text: خد تاكسي أحسن. ده الميدان قدامك.
lines.id: Better take a taxi. There's the square, right in front of you.
lines.literal: take taxi better. this the-square in-front-of-you.

lines.speaker: الراجل:
lines.id: You're welcome. God be with you.

notes: **The phrase على طول means "straight on", and also "right away".** Literally "along the length". With time it means immediately: روحت على طول (I went straight away). With directions it means without turning. The two meanings never get mixed up.
**The word خش means "go in" and is used for "turn".** It's the imperative of the verb خش *khashsh*. A common alternative is حوّد *hawwid* (turn). Both are heard all the time on the streets of Cairo.

**Right and left in Egypt: يمين and شمال.** The word شمال also means "north", and that's where it comes from — in the Arab world, someone facing the sunrise finds north on their left hand. Context separates the two without any trouble.

**The phrase قد إيه means "how much / how far / how long", for distance, size, and time.** بعيدة قد إيه؟ (how far?), كبيرة قد إيه؟ (how big?), حتقعد قد إيه؟ (how long are you staying?). It's one of the most useful questions and one beginners most often overlook.

**The address يا أسطى comes from the Turkish *usta*, "master craftsman".** It's used for drivers, workmen, street vendors, and anyone who works with their hands — respectfully, not condescendingly. For a taxi driver, it's exactly the right word.

**The phrase ربنا معاك is a warm farewell**, literally "our Lord is with you". It's said to someone heading off to something that isn't easy, and accepting all its goodwill is part of learning this language.

grammars.title: The imperative — the shortest form of all
body: The imperative is made by dropping the prefix تـ from the verb form without بـ. Nothing is added; something is taken away.
after: The last three rows are irregular and must be memorized: تعالى (come here), هات (bring), خد (take). All three are among the words you'll hear most in Egypt.

To tell someone not to do something, don't use the imperative but the انت form inside the مـ...ـش wrapper, as in ماتشربش (don't drink), ماتروحش (don't go), ماتنساش (don't forget). It's exactly the ordinary negation pattern covered in unit 10.
A bare imperative sounds harsh. The Egyptian way to soften it isn't to change the verb but to add words: لو سمحت in front, من فضلك at the end, or يا بيه at the very end. Compare اقعد with اتفضل اقعد.

grammars.title: Prepositions of place
body: All the following prepositions can take the person endings you already know from unit four — قدامي، وراك، جنبه.

head: مصري
Say it
Meaning
Example
Meaning of example
rows: between the bank and the school

after: Notice that the preposition في means both "at" and "in"; Egyptian doesn't distinguish them. To stress the inside, people add جوه *guwwa*: جوه الأوضة.
The word على often shortens to عـ in fast speech: عالشمال، عاليمين، عالطول. You'll hear this short form far more often than the long one.

blocks.text: A few Cairo place names will keep coming up and are worth recognizing from the start: وسط البلد *wisṭ il-balad* (Downtown), ميدان التحرير *midaan it-tahriir* (Tahrir Square), الزمالك *iz-Zamaalik*, المعادي *il-Ma‘aadi*, الدقي *id-Do’’i*, مصر الجديدة *Maṣr ig-Gidiida* (Heliopolis), والقلعة *il-’al‘a* (the Citadel).

blocks.title: The word كوبري and the Turkish legacy on the streets
items: The word كوبري (bridge) comes from Turkish *köprü*, and it's one of dozens of Turkish words that have lived in Egyptian since four centuries of Ottoman rule.
Others: أوضة (room, from *oda*), دولاب (wardrobe, from *dolap*), أسطى (master craftsman, from *usta*), جزمة (shoe, from *çizme*), بقشيش (tip, from *bahşiş*), أفندم (sir, from *efendim*).
Some of these words even reached English by other routes — compare *baksheesh* with بقشيش, or *effendi* with أفندم.

sections.title: Asking the way without getting more lost

blocks.text: The hardest part of asking for directions isn't the asking but understanding the answer. The following phrases help you stay in control of the conversation.

head: مصري
Say it
Meaning
rows: could you show me on the map?

blocks.text: The phrase ممكن تورّيني على الخريطة؟ is worth memorizing whole. Spoken directions in Cairo tend to be long, fast, and full of place names you don't know yet; asking to be shown on a map cuts through all of it in one step.

It's on your right, next to the pharmacy.
How far is it from here?
